subject: Variance of predict()ed factor scores inferior to model estimates?

messages.author: 84e6ff87e445f88b
messages.subject: Variance of predict()ed factor scores inferior to model estimates?
parts:
Dear all,

I need to predict() factor scores to use in another software. All runs fine except that the variance of the predicted factor tends to be lower than the model estimate. Even in CFA when the model variance is fixed to 1, the predicted score variance is less than 1 (0.7 in the example below...). I know that prediction is not straightforward, but is there a reason why the mean is spot on and the variance lower in all my examples? Below is a cfa and growth model with lavaan data that shows this.

Many Thanks!

JB


library(lavaan)
library(semTools)
set.seed(12345)
 
#Predict without missing,using origina demo.growth
modelbase <- ' i =~ 1*t1 + 1*t2 + 1*t3 + 1*t4
s =~ 0*t1 + 1*t2 + 2*t3 + 3*t4'
fit <- growth(modelbase, data=Demo.growth)
summary(fit)
pmodelbase=predict(fit) 
mean(pmodelbase[,1]);var(pmodelbase[,1])
mean(pmodelbase[,2]);var(pmodelbase[,2])
#the mean Intercept and slope are exactly like in the model estimate
#the variances are lower, still 90% of model estimates in this example, but about 60%  in my real data
#Any idea why this difference in prediction accuracy between means and variances
 
#OTHER EXAMPLE WITH CFA:
HS.model.bis <- 'visual =~ NA*x1 + x2 + x3
 textual =~ NA*x4 + x5 + x6
 speed =~ NA*x7 + x8 + x9
 visual ~~ 1*visual
 textual ~~ 1*textual
 speed ~~ 1*speed
'
fitbis <- cfa(HS.model.bis, data = HolzingerSwineford1939,meanstructure=T)
summary(fitbis,standardized=T)
pHS.model=predict(fitbis)
mean(pHS.model[,1]);var(pHS.model[,1]) #here the mean is again spot on but he variance, fixed to 1 in the model, is 0.72

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: Variance of predict()ed factor scores inferior to model estimates?
parts:
JB—

     The reason is that what factor software calls “factor scores” are not true factors scores at all.  Factors are typically indeterminate, meaning that they include a component that does not have one specific value.  With true factor scores, this component will be weighted so that it accounts for a share of variance equal to 1 – R2(F, Y), or 1 – the R2 where the observed variables are used to predict the common factor.  The pseudo factor scores produced by factor software omit this component, so you should expect these pseudo factor scores to have variance equal to (1 – R2(F, Y))% of the variance of the factor in your model.  There are other differences, as well.

     If you want to use a factor model but avoid indeterminacy, you need more and better observed variables per factor.  If you want genuine factor scores, it is easy to fabricate the missing component, but remember this component is a vector with no one best set of values, so any particular draw is just one of an infinity of possibilities.  I can refer you to the literature, if you would like to read up.

--Ed Rigdon

If I remember correctly, LISREL transformed its factor scores so that
the variances would match. There is a paper (or report) by Joreskog:

http://www.ssicentral.com/lisrel/techdocs/lvscores.pdf

It is perfectly feasible to mimic this behaviour. But why exactly do we
need this?

Yves.

Dear Edward and Yves,
Many thanks for your answers! Yes, having some references from you Edward would be great (if possible sth that explains it as simply as possible as my equation reading skills are a bit limited). This question of indeterminacy is still a little bit mysterious for me, in particular for latent growth curve as the individual trajectories are like simple regressions, with not much room for indeterminacy? (I know that we can fit similar models in a mixed model framework where there is no latent score). But it will hopefully be clearer with a little bit of reading. Regarding Yves' comment, if the lisrel behaviour is a simple transformation that does not affect the relationship of the extracted factor with other variables then its use seems indeed limited. However, it might be useful in practice to avoid having to explain to reviewers why model and extracted variances are different?
Thanks again for lavaan, it is great!
JB

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Variance of predict()ed factor scores inferior to model estimates?
parts:
Factor indeterminacy originates in the rank problem that is at the root of common factor analysis.  Say you have 4 observed variables loading on 1 common factor.  Then the covariance matrix of the observed variables has rank at most 4--there are at most 4 dimensions of information to be extracted.  The common factor model includes 1 common factor and 4 errors or specific factors, and all of these are independent, making 5 dimensions of information.  How do you turn 4 dimensions of empirical information into 5?  Make the 5 indeterminate.
     The best recent source on factor indeterminacy would be the discussion in Stan Mulaik's indispensible (2010, 2nd ed.) Foundations of Factor Analysis.  Most books on factor-based SEM, including Hoyle's Handbook of SEM are silent.
     Classic literature includes Louis Guttman's (1955) comprehensive paper:
     Guttman, Louis (1955), THE DETERMINACY OF FACTOR SCORE MATRICES WITH IMPLICATIONS FOR FIVE OTHER BASIC PROBLEMS OF COMMON-FACTOR THEORY, British Journal of Statistical Psychology, 8(2), 55-81.
      But there is a brief treatment in Steiger and Schonemann's 
     Schönemann, P.H., & Steiger, J.H. (1976). Regression component 
And there are other sources.  The very first discussion is in Wilson's review of Charles Spearman's The Abilities of Man.  The review was published in Nature in 1928.
--Ed Rigdon
